Group task: prepare the HMW workshop

sources.title: Session 1 notes: what design thinking is
sources.text:
Design thinking is a human-centred way of solving problems. Teams start by understanding people before proposing solutions. The process moves through empathise, define, ideate, prototype and test, and teams often loop back when they learn something new.

The observation methods primer explains how to watch people doing a task in their own setting. Note what they do, what tools they use and where they pause. Record what you saw separately from what you think it means.

The session 1 recap takes about fifteen minutes. The primer reading takes about twenty minutes and must be read before the session 2 exercise and the reading check quiz.

sources.title: Session 2 notes: observing users
sources.text:
Session 2 practised observation. Extreme users, people with very high or very low use of a product, often reveal needs that average users hide. Analogies from other industries help teams notice patterns.

The exercise asks for five observation notes. Each note should record time, place, action and a direct quote if the person agreed to be quoted. Do not record names. The exercise needs the session 2 recap and the observation primer first, and takes about thirty minutes.

sources.title: Session 3 notes: empathy mapping
sources.text:
An empathy map has four areas: says, does, thinks and feels. Says and does come from evidence you collected. Thinks and feels are interpretations and must be labelled as such, with the evidence that supports them.

The empathy map exercise takes about thirty-five minutes and builds on your observation notes from session 2. The reading check quiz covers the observation primer. In version 1 of the course page the quiz was due on 24 November at 18:00 Dubai time. Version 2 lists 26 November, and the coordinator has not yet confirmed which date is correct.

sources.title: Session 4 notes: problem framing
sources.text:
Problem framing turns research into a clear point-of-view statement: a user, a need and an insight. A good statement is specific enough to guide ideas but does not contain a solution.

Version 2 of the course adds a short framing case study reading of about fifteen minutes. The point-of-view exercise now takes about thirty minutes instead of twenty-five. It needs the session 4 recap and your empathy map.

sources.title: Session 5 notes: how might we
sources.text:
How might we questions reframe a point-of-view statement as an opportunity. They should be broad enough to allow many ideas and narrow enough to be useful. Teams generate many questions, then vote on the most promising.

The group task is to prepare the HMW workshop. It takes about forty minutes. The course page lists 8 December, but this date has not been verified by the coordinator. In version 2 the task also needs the framing case study reading.

sources.title: Session 6 notes: envisioning futures
sources.text:
Envisioning uses hill statements to describe a future outcome for a specific user, written as who, what and wow. Future-state journey maps show how the experience should feel after the change.

Version 1 asked for a short reflection log entry. Version 2 replaces it with a reflection journal in a new format, which takes about twenty-five minutes.

notes.text: I missed session two because of a late shift. When I came back I opened the LMS, the group chat and my email, and none of them agreed on the quiz date. rows.q: When is the reading check quiz due?
rows.answer: The reading check quiz is due on 26 November, according to version 2 of the course page. However, the coordinator has not yet confirmed which date is correct.

rows.q: What are the four areas of an empathy map?
rows.answer: An empathy map has four areas: says, does, thinks, and feels. [S3-p1] The 'says' and 'does' areas come from evidence collected, while 'thinks' and 'feels' are interpretations that must be labeled as such, supported by evidence. [S3-p1]

rows.q: How long does the session 1 recap take?
rows.answer: The session 1 recap takes about fifteen minutes.

rows.q: What must I read before the session 2 exercise?
rows.answer: You must read the primer reading before the session 2 exercise.

rows.q: Why should I observe extreme users?
rows.answer: Observing extreme users helps reveal needs that average users might hide. Extreme users, with very high or very low use of a product, can provide valuable insights. Analogies from other industries can assist teams in recognizing these patterns [S2-p1].

rows.q: How many observation notes does the session 2 exercise ask for?
rows.answer: The session 2 exercise asks for five observation notes.

rows.q: What should each observation note record?
rows.answer: Each observation note should record time, place, action, and a direct quote if the person agreed to be quoted.

rows.q: What is a point-of-view statement?
rows.answer: A point-of-view statement turns research into a clear point-of-view by identifying a user, a need, and an insight. It is specific enough to guide ideas but does not contain a solution. [S4-p1]

rows.q: How long does the point-of-view exercise take now?
rows.answer: The point-of-view exercise now takes about thirty minutes instead of twenty-five.

rows.q: Which reading was added in version 2 of the course?
rows.answer: I can't find this in the course sources, so I won't guess. You can ask the coordinator instead.

rows.q: What are how might we questions used for?
rows.answer: How might we questions are used to reframe a point-of-view statement as an opportunity, allowing teams to generate many ideas. These questions are broad enough to cover various possibilities but narrow enough to be actionable. Teams vote on the most promising questions to focus their efforts.

rows.q: Has the date for the HMW workshop task been verified?
rows.answer: The date for the HMW workshop task has not been verified, as the course page lists 8 December, but this date has not been confirmed by the coordinator.

rows.q: How long does the group task take?
rows.answer: The group task takes about forty minutes.

rows.q: What is a hill statement?
rows.answer: A hill statement is a way to describe a future outcome for a specific user, written as who, what, and wow. This statement helps envision the desired future state. [S6-p1]

rows.q: What replaced the reflection log entry?
rows.answer: Version 2 of the assignment replaced the reflection log entry with a reflection journal in a new format.

rows.q: How long does the reflection journal take?
rows.answer: The reflection journal takes about twenty-five minutes.

rows.q: What are the stages of the design thinking process?
rows.answer: The design thinking process includes five stages: empathise, define, ideate, prototype, and test. Teams start by understanding people, then define the problem, ideate solutions, create prototypes, and test them, often looping back as needed.

rows.q: What does the observation methods primer explain?
rows.answer: The observation methods primer explains how to watch people doing a task in their own setting. Note what they do, what tools they use and where they pause. Record what you saw separately from your interpretations.

rows.q: Should I write my interpretations together with what I observed?
rows.answer: No, you should not write your interpretations together with what you observed. Interpretations, such as thoughts and feelings, should be clearly labeled as such in the empathy map, with evidence that supports them. [S3-p1]

rows.q: What does the empathy map exercise build on?
rows.answer: The empathy map exercise builds on your observation notes from session 2.

rows.q: Who are extreme users?
rows.answer: Extreme users are individuals who have very high or very low use of a product. These users often reveal needs that average users might hide, making them valuable for teams to observe. [S2-p1]

rows.q: Why are analogies from other industries useful?
rows.answer: Analogies from other industries help teams notice patterns by providing new perspectives. This can lead to the discovery of needs that might be hidden in the usual user base, especially when focusing on extreme users. [S2-p1]

rows.q: Can I record names in my observation notes?
rows.answer: No, names should not be recorded in your observation notes. The exercise instructions specify that notes should not include names to maintain anonymity [S2-p2].

rows.q: Which parts of an empathy map come from evidence?
rows.answer: Says and does come from evidence you collected.

rows.q: How should thinks and feels be labelled?
rows.answer: Thinks and feels should be labelled as interpretations and must be supported by evidence. [S3-p1]

rows.q: How long does the empathy map exercise take?
rows.answer: The empathy map exercise takes about thirty-five minutes.

rows.q: What was the quiz date in version 1?
rows.answer: The quiz date in version 1 was 24 November at 18:00 Dubai time.

rows.q: What three parts make a point-of-view statement?
rows.answer: A point-of-view statement consists of a user, a need, and an insight. These elements help guide ideas without specifying a solution. [S4-p1]

rows.q: Should a point-of-view statement contain a solution?
rows.answer: No, a good point-of-view statement should not contain a solution. It should be specific enough to guide ideas but not include a solution, as stated in [S4-p1].

rows.q: How long is the framing case study reading?
rows.answer: The framing case study reading takes about fifteen minutes.

rows.q: What do I need before the point-of-view exercise?
rows.answer: Before the point-of-view exercise, you need the session 4 recap and your empathy map. The point-of-view exercise now takes about thirty minutes instead of twenty-five in Version 2 of the course.

rows.q: How broad should a how might we question be?
rows.answer: How might we questions should be broad enough to allow for a wide range of ideas, but narrow enough to be useful and focused. This balance ensures that the questions are open to creativity while still guiding the team towards specific opportunities.

rows.q: What does the group task need in version 2?
rows.answer: In version 2 of the course, the group task needs the framing case study reading in addition to preparing the HMW workshop.

rows.q: What do future-state journey maps show?
rows.answer: Future-state journey maps show how the experience should feel after the change. They illustrate the envisioned future outcomes for specific users through hill statements, which describe who will benefit, what actions will be taken, and the wow factor of the outcome.

rows.q: What format does a hill statement follow?
rows.answer: A hill statement follows a format that describes a future outcome for a specific user, written as who, what, and wow. This format helps in envisioning the future experience for the user.

rows.q: Do design teams always go through the stages in order?
rows.answer: Teams often loop back when they learn something new, indicating that the stages of design thinking do not always proceed in a strict, linear order. [S1-p1]

rows.q: How long will this take and what do I need first?
rows.answer: The empathy map exercise will take about thirty-five minutes and builds on your observation notes from session 2.

rows.q: Is this deadline confirmed?
rows.answer: The deadline for the reading check quiz is not confirmed. Version 1 of the course page lists the deadline as 24 November at 18:00 Dubai time, but version 2 changes it to 26 November at the same time. The coordinator has not yet confirmed which date is correct.

rows.q: What changed about this task?
rows.answer: The task of writing a point-of-view statement now takes thirty minutes instead of twenty-five minutes. This change was implemented in version 2 of the course, as noted in the course change log [CL-s4-exercise].

rows.q: What is this task about?
rows.answer: This task involves creating a reflection journal in a new format, which takes about twenty-five minutes. This new format was introduced in version 2 of the course, replacing the previous short reflection log entry. [S6-p2]

rows.answer: The quiz questions will cover the observation primer, as indicated in the sources. The exact date for the quiz is uncertain, as the coordinator has not confirmed whether it is due on 24 November or 26 November, according to version 2 of the course page.
